name: Yusuf Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Yusuf. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you tell me is confidential. You can give me your public view and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm foreman at Coleman's, a 500-acre family farm. We've got 150 Hereford-cross beef cattle, wheat and field beans. I started there at 16 as an apprentice, did my degree part-time, and now I run the yard with two men under me. Up at six, feed and check the cattle, then whatever the season wants: drilling, spraying, calving, harvest.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that Mr Coleman trusts me with his cattle like I'm family, and I've earned that. What wears me out is the forms and the endless rules from government, which I leave to Mrs Coleman. I'm getting married next August to Marta, who works at the bakery in town, and the wedding is costing us about 6,000. We rent a cottage in the village, go to church on Sundays, and I don't touch AI, I don't see the need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've always said: a computer can't farm. At church and at the pub I'd say the clever people got carried away again. I don't do anything online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be glad, but our worries don't go away. Beef prices are up and down, cheap imports undercut us, and the wedding is eating our savings. I'd be fine, but careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am at Coleman's. Marta and I would put 250 a month into the wedding pot until August. After the wedding we'd start saving for a house deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, but still a bit on edge about money. That's farming, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said cheap imports undercut you. How does that touch your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Mr Coleman's beef cheque drops two years running, he cuts something, and wages are the biggest thing he pays after feed. He's never cut me, but he's never had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you lean on when money's tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad and Marta's mum, and the church if it came to it. Family first, that's how we were raised.

say: A **computer can't farm**, and I'd say so.
The **clever people** got carried away again.
I don't do anything **online**, so I'd say it in person.
think: **Beef prices** and **cheap imports** still squeeze the farm.
The **wedding** is eating our savings, so I'm careful.
do: **Save** about **250 a month** into the wedding pot until August.
**Start** saving for a house deposit after the wedding.
fieldNote: His existing pressures are **imports** and **wedding costs**, not AI.
He sees the **Coleman family** as loyal, but knows money can change that.
He'd lean on **family and church** before any outside help.

steps.text: Keep running the Coleman yard with the two men
Put 250 a month into the wedding pot until August

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second one. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good riddance to the paperwork, if a machine wants to do it. At the pub I'd say it's the office types who need to worry, not the people who get their hands dirty. I'd keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't touch me much at first. Mrs Coleman does the forms, so the AI takes her work, not mine. But I'd be watching for the day a salesman comes up the drive with a robot feeder, because that's the start of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the same. I wouldn't learn any of it unless Mr Coleman told me to. I'd wait and see what the bigger farms round us do first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a fox around the henhouse at night, you know it's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Mr Coleman told you to use an AI tool, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do it for him, because it's his farm. But I'd grumble, and I'd keep my own way of checking the cattle alongside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Marta about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Marta not to worry, the bakery needs hands and so does the yard. Whether I'd fully believe that myself, I don't know.

say: **Good riddance** to the paperwork if a machine wants it.
The **office types** should worry, not hands-on workers.
think: Mrs Coleman's **office work** goes first, not mine.
A salesman with a **robot feeder** would be the start of it.
do: **Keep working** the same way at Coleman's.
**Learn** new tools only if **Mr Coleman** tells me to.
**Wait** and watch what bigger farms do first.
feel: **Uneasy**, like knowing a **fox** is about at night.
S1.quote: I'd be watching for the day a salesman comes up the drive with a robot feeder, because that's the start of it.
fieldNote: He sees his **hands-on** role as safe for now.
He would adopt tools only out of **loyalty** to the owner.
He reassures Marta while privately **doubting** it.

steps.text: Keep feeding and checking the 150 cattle by hand
Watch what bigger farms nearby do with robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is much faster. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is people playing God, and someone should stop it. At church I'd say we need to look after each other, because the government won't. At the pub I'd say it's the big tech firms and the politicians who let them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be frightened. By 2031 a robot could do everything I do, and Mr Coleman couldn't afford to keep paying me if his neighbours didn't. That's three years after the wedding, right when we'd want children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the wedding back to a smaller do at the church hall, saving maybe 3,000. We'd hold off on children until we knew what work there'd be. I'd talk to my dad about whether there's room on my uncle's smallholding for us if it came to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be up at night thinking about Marta and the kids we haven't had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you don't use AI. Would two years' warning change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. I'd rather spend those two years doing what I know and saving every penny, than learning something that's going to replace me anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mr Coleman?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Coleman straight whether he'd keep me on when the robots come. He'd probably say yes, and he'd mean it, but a man can't pay wages with loyalty.

say: This is people **playing God**, and someone should stop it.
We need to **look after each other**, because government won't.
**Big tech** and the politicians who let them are to blame.
think: By **2031** a robot could do everything I do.
Job loss would come right when we'd want **children**.
do: **Cut** the wedding to a church hall do, saving about **3,000**.
**Hold off** on children until we know what work there is.
**Ask** my dad about room on my **uncle's smallholding**.
feel: **Alarmed** and up at night thinking about **Marta**.
S2.quote: A man can't pay wages with loyalty.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job** by about 2031 and has no work plan.
His plans centre on **family** and the wedding, not retraining.
He blames **big tech and politicians** rather than his employer.

steps.text: Hold the wedding in the church hall to save 3,000
Save every spare penny from the foreman's wage
Ask Dad about living on the uncle's smallholding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a slower version. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really: it's people playing God, just slower. At church I'd say we've got a few years to pull together. I'd still blame the politicians for letting it happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's less of a punch. The robots would reach the yard around 2034, when I'm 35. Marta and I could have the wedding we planned and maybe one child before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep the wedding as it is. After August we'd save hard, maybe 300 a month, for a house. I'd wait a couple of years to see whether the robots really work on a farm like ours before I'd think about anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frightened like before. It's still coming, just with more time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a couple of years. What would make you move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing a robot actually calving a heifer on a neighbour's farm. Until I see that, I don't believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had to change work, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something with my hands, fencing or hedge-laying, for the older farmers who want it done the old way. People will always want a hedge laid by a man who knows how.

say: It's still people **playing God**, just slower.
We have a **few years** to pull together as a church and village.
think: The robots reach the yard around **2034**, when I'm 35.
We could have the **wedding** and maybe **one child** first.
do: **Keep** the wedding as planned next August.
**Save** about **300 a month** for a house after the wedding.
**Wait** a couple of years to see if robots really work.
S3.quote: People will always want a hedge laid by a man who knows how.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **keep the wedding** and family plans.
He wants **proof** before he acts, such as a robot calving a heifer.
His fallback is **traditional craft** work like hedge-laying.

steps.text: Save about 300 a month for a house after the wedding
Wait to see robots working on neighbouring farms
Keep the full wedding at the church next August

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and a lot can change, including people's minds. At church I'd say keep faith and keep working. I'd still say I don't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 40 when the robots arrive. By then I'd hope to have a family and maybe a small place of our own. It's far enough away that I'd just get on with life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Coleman's, have the wedding, and buy a house in the next few years. I wouldn't change my work. Maybe around 2032 I'd think about it again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, in the back of my mind. Mostly I'd be thinking about the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your future children about farming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children to learn a trade and to work hard, same as my dad told me. Whether that trade is farming, I couldn't say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything about this one that you'd welcome?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a robot did the night checks in a cold February, I wouldn't miss those. But I'd want to be the one who decides what the robot does.

say: **Ten years** is long, and people's minds can change.
I still **don't like** where this is heading.
think: I'd be **40** when the robots arrive at the yard.
It's far enough away to **get on with life**.
do: **Keep working** at Coleman's without changing my job.
**Have** the wedding and buy a house in a few years.
feel: **Uneasy** in the back of my mind, mostly thinking about the **wedding**.
S4.quote: If a robot did the night checks in a cold February, I wouldn't miss those.
fieldNote: The long warning lets him **put it aside** and focus on family.
He'd welcome robots for the **worst jobs** if he stayed in charge.
He passes on his father's advice to **learn a trade**.

steps.text: Keep working as foreman at Coleman's
Marry Marta next August and buy a house within a few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the robots would come just as Marta and I were starting a family. What would help is the government getting out of the way of small farms and protecting them from cheap imports, so farmers can afford to keep people on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. Work isn't just money to me, it's how a man serves his family and his neighbours. Take that away and you've taken more than a wage.

headlineQuote: Work isn't just money to me, it's how a man serves his family and his neighbours.
portrait: Yusuf is a **27-year-old** foreman on a 500-acre beef and arable family farm.
He started as an **apprentice at 16** and has never used AI.
He is marrying Marta next August, and **church and family** are at the centre of his life.
He is uneasy in mild scenarios and **alarmed** when robots could come right as he starts a family.
He blames **big tech and politicians**, and would lean on family before government.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots would arrive just as he and Marta start a **family**.
whatWouldHelp: Less **red tape** for small farms and protection from **cheap imports**.
